tiles.title: Measures of Center and Spread
tiles.summary: Introduces the three measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and three measures of spread (range, variance, standard deviation) using a seven-order QuickRide delivery dataset. Emphasises when the median is more representative than the mean, and why standard deviation is more interpretable than variance.

steps.title: What's a typical delivery time?
steps.lede: Seven QuickRide orders came in at 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80 minutes. Before you can say anything useful, you need one number that answers "what's typical here?" — and there are three ways to find it.

blocks.caption: Seven delivery times sorted smallest to largest. Mean ≈ 30.9 min (pulled up by ORD-007), median = 22 min (middle value), mode = 22 min (appears twice).

blocks.text: The **sample mean** is the sum of all values divided by the count. For these seven orders: 18 + 20 + 22 + 22 + 26 + 28 + 80 = 216, and 216 ÷ 7 ≈ **30.9 minutes**.

The **median** is the middle value of the sorted list. With seven orders, the fourth value is the middle one — that's **22 minutes**. If there were an even number of orders, you'd average the two middle values.

steps.title: Mode and when the mean misleads
steps.lede: The mean and median both describe center, but they react very differently when one value is far from the rest.

blocks.text: The **mode** is the value that appears most often. In this batch, 22 minutes appears twice while every other time appears once — so **22 minutes** is the mode. A dataset can have more than one mode.

Notice the gap: mean ≈ 30.9 min, but median = mode = 22 min. The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them. That single 80-minute delivery pulls the mean almost 9 minutes above where six of the seven orders actually sit. When a dataset has one unusually large value, the median is usually the better "typical" number to report.

steps.title: Choose the right center
steps.lede: Pick the measure that best represents a typical delivery time for this batch.

steps.title: Compute mean, median, and mode
steps.lede: Use the seven QuickRide delivery times to compute all three measures of center, then decide which one best represents a typical delivery.

steps.title: How spread out are the delivery times?
steps.lede: Knowing the median is 22 minutes doesn't say whether all orders are close to that or wildly scattered. Spread measures fill that gap.

blocks.text: Most of the seven delivery times (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) cluster fairly close together — but one sits far away. The **range** is the simplest spread measure: largest minus smallest. Here that's 80 − 18 = **62 minutes**.

The **variance** measures the average squared distance from the mean. With a mean of about 30.9 minutes, the seven squared deviations sum to about 2 886.9. Dividing by n − 1 = 6 gives a variance of about **481.1 minutes²**.

blocks.title: From raw values to standard deviation
blocks.alt_text: Five-step flowchart: subtract mean → square → sum → divide by n-1 (variance, minutes²) → square root (standard deviation, minutes).

steps.title: Standard deviation and the range's blind spot
steps.lede: The variance is useful for calculation, but its units are squared. The standard deviation brings the number back to the original units — and the range has a hidden weakness.

blocks.text: The **standard deviation** is the square root of the variance: √481.1 ≈ **21.9 minutes** — roughly how far a typical delivery time sits from the 30.9-minute mean. It's in the same units as the data, making it easier to interpret than the variance (minutes²).

The **range** (62 minutes) uses only the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread. Variance and standard deviation use every observation's distance from the mean, so they capture whether the middle values are bunched or scattered.

steps.lede: Watch the squared-deviation method in action, then see why dividing by n − 1 gives a better estimate for a sample.

bridge.after: The clip never covers the range. Devspace adds it: the range uses only the two extreme values, so it can't say whether the rest of the data is bunched or scattered.

steps.lede: Choose the statement that best explains the range's main limitation as a spread measure.

steps.lede: Using the same seven delivery times, compute the range, the sample variance (dividing by n − 1), and the standard deviation. Then state what the standard deviation means in minutes.

steps.title: Center and spread: what you've learned
steps.lede: Three measures of center, three measures of spread — and a clear rule for which to use.

blocks.text: Mean, median, and mode all answer "what's typical," but the mean is pulled by extreme values while the median is not — so check for unusually large values before reporting a single center number.

Range, variance, and standard deviation all quantify spread. The range uses only the two extremes; variance and standard deviation use every observation's distance from the mean. Standard deviation is in the original units, making it the most directly interpretable.

blocks.title: Up next: Distribution Shape and Outliers
blocks.text: You've seen how a single extreme value pulls the mean away from the median. Next, you'll learn to describe the overall shape of a distribution — whether it's symmetric or lopsided — and develop a principled approach to identifying and reasoning about outliers.

remediation_steps.title: Mean vs median: which one to trust
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked which measure best represents a typical delivery time. Here's the contrast that makes it clear.

blocks.text: The **mean** sums all values and divides by the count: 216 ÷ 7 ≈ 30.9 minutes. The **median** is the middle value of the sorted list: the fourth of seven sorted values is 22 minutes.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median. The single 80-minute delivery pulls the mean to 30.9 — nearly 9 minutes above where six of the seven orders actually sit. When one value is unusually large, the median (22 minutes here) is the more representative "typical" delivery time.

remediation_steps.title: Computing mean, median, and mode step by step
remediation_steps.lede: The hands-on asked you to compute all three measures. Here's each calculation laid out clearly.

blocks.text: **Mean:** add all seven values (18 + 20 + 22 + 22 + 26 + 28 + 80 = 216) and divide by 7 → ≈ **30.9 minutes**. **Median:** sort the values; the fourth (middle) value is **22 minutes**. **Mode:** 22 minutes appears twice, every other value once → mode = **22 minutes**.

remediation_steps.title: Why the range misses the full picture
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about the range's main limitation. Here's the contrast that makes it concrete.

blocks.text: The range (62 minutes) is based only on the two most extreme values — 80 and 18 — and ignores how the rest of the data are spread. Imagine all six non-outlier deliveries were exactly 22 minutes: the range would still be 62, even though the data is far less scattered. Variance and standard deviation use every observation's distance from the mean, so they capture that difference.

remediation_steps.title: Range, variance, and standard deviation step by step
remediation_steps.lede: The hands-on asked you to compute all three spread measures. Here's each calculation laid out clearly.

blocks.text: **Range:** 80 − 18 = **62 minutes** (largest minus smallest). **Variance:** sum the squared deviations from the mean (≈ 30.9) and divide by n − 1 = 6 → ≈ **481.1 minutes²**. **Standard deviation:** √481.1 ≈ **21.9 minutes** — the typical distance of a delivery time from the mean, in the original units.

The range only looks at the two extremes; variance and standard deviation take every observation into account. Standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the data (minutes), while variance is in squared units (minutes²) — making standard deviation the easier one to interpret directly.

tiles.title: A/B Test Structure and Lift
tiles.summary: Introduces the structure of a randomised A/B test (control group, treatment group, metric) and the concept of lift (relative improvement) using QuickRide's checkout-button experiment. Learners identify the parts of an experiment and compute lift from control and treatment conversion rates.

steps.title: Two groups, one metric, one baseline
steps.lede: QuickRide's product team wants to know whether a redesigned checkout button gets more users to complete an order. Rather than guess, they run a controlled test — showing each user one version at random and measuring what happens.

blocks.text: Randomised experiments: control vs treatment

Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called **experiments**. When the assignment includes randomisation, it is called a **randomised experiment**. Researchers randomly assign cases to a **control group** and a **treatment group** so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

**A/B testing** works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (**control, or A**) and a modified version (**variation, or B**). Engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline — the control. For the checkout button: the existing button is A, the redesigned button is B, and the metric compared is the share of each group that completes an order.

steps.title: Turning raw rates into a single comparison figure
steps.lede: The checkout test is done: the control button converted 20 % of users, the redesigned button converted 22 %. Those two numbers need to be turned into a comparison that's easy to talk about — that's where lift comes in.

blocks.text: Relative improvement (lift)

**Relative improvement (lift)** is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate. For example, a 10 % relative improvement over a 25 % baseline means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5 %. Relative improvement describes the variation's change **as a percentage of the baseline's rate** — not as a percentage-point difference.

Applying that to the checkout test: treatment rate 22 % minus control rate 20 % is a **2-percentage-point** absolute difference. As a percentage of the 20 % baseline: 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = **10 % lift**. The redesigned button produced a 10 % relative improvement over the original.

result_of.sql: SELECT "group", users, conversions, conversion_rate FROM ab_test_summary WHERE "group" = 'control'
SELECT "group", users, conversions, conversion_rate FROM ab_test_summary WHERE "group" = 'treatment'

blocks.takeaway: Absolute difference: 0.22 − 0.20 = 0.02 (2 pp). Lift: 0.02 ÷ 0.20 × 100 = 10 % — the redesigned button produced a 10 % relative improvement over the baseline.

blocks.text: Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a **positive**, **negative**, or **neutral** effect compared with the baseline (control). A **positive lift** means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test. A **negative lift** means it came out below. A **neutral** result means the rates were effectively the same.

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Every A/B test has the same three parts, and lift turns the raw rates into one interpretable figure.

blocks.text: Every A/B test has a **control group**, a **treatment group**, and the **measure** being compared between them. The treatment group's result is compared against the control — the baseline. Analysing the results means determining whether the variation had a **positive, negative, or neutral** effect. **Lift** puts the observed difference into one figure: a positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test; a negative lift means it came out below.

blocks.title: Up next: Sample Size and Statistical Significance
blocks.text: You can now compute lift — but how do you know whether a 10 % lift is a real signal or just random variation? The next tile introduces the tools that tell you whether your A/B test result is trustworthy.

remediation_steps.title: What makes an experiment randomised?
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked you to distinguish a randomised experiment from a non-randomised study. Here's the key contrast.

blocks.text: Studies where researchers **assign** treatments to cases are called **experiments**. When that assignment includes **randomisation**, it is a **randomised experiment**. Randomly assigning cases to a control group and a treatment group evens out differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled — that's what makes the comparison fair.

A non-randomised study lets participants choose their own group, or assigns them by convenience. Without random assignment, the two groups may differ in ways that affect the outcome — so you can't be sure the treatment caused any difference you observe. In the checkout-button test, users are randomly shown one version or the other, which is what makes it a randomised experiment.

remediation_steps.title: Identifying the groups and metric in an A/B test
remediation_steps.lede: The hands-on asked you to identify the control group, treatment group, and the metric being compared. Here's how to read the table.

blocks.text: In the user records table, the **`group`** column tells you which arm each user was assigned to: `'control'` for the original button (A) and `'treatment'` for the redesigned button (B). The **`converted`** column records the metric: 1 if the user completed an order, 0 if not. The metric being compared between the two groups is the **share of users who converted** — the conversion rate.

remediation_steps.title: Classifying a test outcome: positive, negative, or neutral
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked you to classify an A/B test outcome. Here's the rule.

blocks.text: Analysing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a **positive**, **negative**, or **neutral** effect compared with the baseline (control). A **positive lift** means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test. A **negative lift** means it came out below. A **neutral** result means the rates were effectively the same.

remediation_steps.title: Computing lift step by step
remediation_steps.lede: The hands-on asked you to compute lift. Here's the calculation laid out clearly.

blocks.text: **Lift formula:** (treatment rate − control rate) ÷ control rate × 100. For the checkout test: (0.22 − 0.20) ÷ 0.20 × 100 = **10 % lift**. This is a relative improvement — it expresses the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate, not as a raw percentage-point difference.

Three cases to check your function against: (1) control=0.20, treatment=0.22 → **+10 % (positive)**. (2) control=0.25, treatment=0.20 → **−20 % (negative)**. (3) control=0.30, treatment=0.30 → **0 % (neutral)**. A positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's; a negative lift means it came out below.

tiles.title: Integrating SQL, Spreadsheets, and pandas
tiles.summary: Apply already-learned SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas skills to the QuickRide capstone project: retrieve last quarter's orders with a multi-clause SELECT, summarise the delivery sheet with a PivotTable and COUNTIFS, clean and aggregate orders in pandas, and model the two-table relationship with correct primary and foreign keys.

steps.title: One SELECT statement: JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY together
steps.lede: The first step of the QuickRide capstone is retrieving last quarter's delivery data. All the SQL clauses you already know — JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY — can live in a single SELECT statement.

blocks.text: Combining clauses in one query

A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query. In the capstone, that means one statement can filter orders down to last quarter's rows **and** group the result by zone — no separate steps needed.

An INNER JOIN can be included in that same FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table **before** WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied. In the capstone, the `orders` and `drivers` tables are joined in the FROM clause first; the WHERE and GROUP BY then narrow and group the combined rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.zone,
       AVG(o.delivery_time) AS avg_delivery_time
FROM   orders o
       INNER JOIN drivers d
           ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= '2026-04-01'
  AND  o.order_date <  '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY o.zone;

annotations.text: FROM + INNER JOIN: combines each order row with its matching driver row first.
WHERE: narrows the combined rows to last quarter (2026-04-01 to 2026-06-30).
GROUP BY: groups the filtered rows by zone so AVG gives one value per zone.

steps.title: Clause order: join first, filter next, group last
steps.lede: The capstone query uses the same SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY you already know — aimed at QuickRide's own tables and date range.

blocks.text: In the capstone query, the INNER JOIN in the FROM clause combines each order row with its matching driver row first. The WHERE clause then narrows those combined rows to orders placed between 2026-04-01 and 2026-06-30. Finally, GROUP BY groups what remains by zone, so AVG(delivery_time) returns one average per zone. None of this is new syntax — it is the same clauses already learned, applied to QuickRide's own tables.

blocks.text: Building a PivotTable from the delivery sheet

A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values. Fields can be dragged between areas to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, `zone` and `shift` (both non-numeric) default to Rows, while `delivery_time` (numeric) goes to Values.

COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]…) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells where **all** criteria are met. In the capstone, `COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45")` counts how many Ikeja deliveries exceeded 45 minutes.

steps.title: Cleaning and grouping the capstone orders in pandas
steps.lede: Once orders are retrieved, pandas handles cleaning and aggregation. isna()/dropna() remove missing delivery times; groupby().mean() produces one average per zone.

blocks.text: Detecting and removing missing values

isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values — or fillna() replaces them with a specified value. In the capstone, `orders['delivery_time'].isna()` flags rows with no delivery time recorded; those rows are then removed with dropna() before any aggregation.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure. An aggregation reduces each group to one summary value per column. In the capstone, `orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()` splits the cleaned orders by zone and returns one mean delivery time per zone.

result_of.sql: SELECT zone, AVG(delivery_time) AS mean_delivery_time FROM ds_pandas_orders WHERE delivery_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY zone ORDER BY zone

after.caption: After dropna() + groupby('zone').mean() — one mean per zone

steps.title: Primary keys, foreign keys, and one-to-many in the capstone
steps.lede: The capstone spans two tables — Orders and Drivers. Before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted, the key columns and their relationship need to be correctly identified.

blocks.text: Primary keys and foreign keys

A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references. In the capstone, the Drivers table needs a column that uniquely identifies each driver, and the Orders table needs a column whose values must match one of those driver identifiers.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side — for example, one department has many employees. In the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table. In the capstone, one driver can appear in many orders: the same one-to-many pattern.

blocks.title: Capstone data model: Drivers (1) → Orders (many)

blocks.text: In the capstone: Drivers has `driver_id` as its primary key, uniquely identifying each driver row. Orders has its own primary key, `order_id`, plus a `driver_id` column that is a foreign key — its values must match a `driver_id` that already exists in Drivers. Since one driver delivers many orders, this is a one-to-many relationship: one row on the Drivers ('one') side relates to many rows on the Orders ('many') side.

remediation_steps.title: Where does the INNER JOIN go in a SELECT statement?
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked where an INNER JOIN fits inside a SELECT. Here's the key rule.

blocks.text: An INNER JOIN is placed in the **FROM clause** of a SELECT statement — not in WHERE or GROUP BY. The FROM clause (including any JOINs) runs first, combining matching rows from both tables. The WHERE clause then filters those combined rows, and GROUP BY groups what remains. In the capstone query, `FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id` combines the two tables before any filtering or grouping.

A common mistake is placing the JOIN condition in the WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE o.driver_id = d.driver_id`). While some databases accept this older syntax, the standard and clearer approach is `INNER JOIN … ON` in the FROM clause, which makes the join explicit and keeps the WHERE clause for row filtering only.

remediation_steps.title: How COUNTIFS applies multiple criteria
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked how COUNTIFS handles more than one criterion. Here's the key rule.

blocks.text: COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2) counts only the rows where **all** criteria are met simultaneously. Each criteria_range/criteria pair is evaluated independently, and only rows that pass every pair are counted. In the capstone, `COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45")` counts rows where the zone is Ikeja **and** the delivery time exceeds 45 minutes — both conditions must hold.

COUNTIFS is not the same as two separate COUNTIF calls added together. Adding two COUNTIF results would count rows that meet either criterion, not both. COUNTIFS enforces all criteria at once, so the count is always ≤ the count from any single criterion alone.

remediation_steps.title: PivotTable field placement and COUNTIFS together
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about executing the full capstone spreadsheet analysis step. Here are the two key rules.

blocks.text: When you add a field to a PivotTable, the tool places it based on its data type: **non-numeric fields** (like zone and shift) default to Rows, **date/time fields** default to Columns, and **numeric fields** (like delivery_time) default to Values. You can drag any field between Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, dragging `shift` from Rows to Columns turns the layout into a zone-by-shift grid.

remediation_steps.title: Cleaning and aggregating: isna()/dropna() then groupby().mean()
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about the full clean-and-aggregate workflow. Here are the two steps.

blocks.text: isna() returns a boolean mask showing which values are missing (NaN). dropna() removes rows with missing values; fillna(value) replaces them. In the capstone, `orders["delivery_time"].isna()` identifies which orders have no recorded delivery time; dropna() removes those rows before any aggregation runs.

A groupby operation splits data into groups, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results. An aggregation reduces each group to one summary value. In the capstone, `orders.groupby("zone")["delivery_time"].mean()` splits the cleaned orders by zone and returns one mean delivery time per zone — an aggregation.

remediation_steps.title: The one-to-many relationship between Drivers and Orders
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about the one-to-many relationship in the capstone. Here is the key rule.

blocks.text: In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the "one" side relates to many rows on the "many" side. The foreign key is placed on the "many" side. In the capstone, one driver (Drivers table, "one" side) can appear in many orders (Orders table, "many" side), so `driver_id` as a foreign key sits in the Orders table — the same pattern as CustID sitting in the Order table.

A common mistake is placing the foreign key on the "one" side. The foreign key always goes on the "many" side — the table that can have multiple rows for the same related entity. In the capstone, Orders (many orders per driver) holds the `driver_id` foreign key, not Drivers.

steps.title: Running describe() on the capstone delivery data
steps.lede: With cleaned, modelled data, the business question needs actual numbers: how late are deliveries, by zone? describe() gives the full summary in one call.

blocks.text: Getting the summary statistics

describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame — count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max. In the capstone, running describe() on a zone's `delivery_time` column returns that full summary in one call, without writing separate mean() or std() calls.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them. When the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful. In the capstone, a handful of unusually long deliveries in a zone can pull the mean upward while the median stays closer to the typical delivery.

steps.title: Choosing mean or median for the business question
steps.lede: describe() gives the full summary; deciding which statistic actually answers the business question depends on whether extreme values are skewing that particular column.

blocks.text: Running describe() on Ikeja's `delivery_time` column returns a mean of 52 minutes and a median of 38 minutes. A handful of deliveries in that zone took over three hours — a stalled vehicle, a wrong address — and the mean is pulled up by those extreme observations, while the median stays at 38 minutes. (These numbers reflect the full dataset; in the visible sample, extreme deliveries extend beyond what is shown.)

The capstone's business question is which zones miss the delivery-time target and by how much — which calls for judging a **typical** delivery against that target, not one skewed by a few rare extremes. So the median is the more useful number here. describe() gives both; the analyst's job is to choose the one that answers the question.

steps.title: Two patterns for multi-panel figures in matplotlib
steps.lede: The findings now need a visualisation set a stakeholder can look at. matplotlib offers two patterns for placing several charts in one figure.

blocks.text: Pattern 1: plt.subplots(2, 2) — a 2×2 grid

`fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` creates one Figure containing a 2×2 grid of Axes, so several charts can share one figure. Each axes is addressed by its row and column index — `axs[0, 0]`, `axs[0, 1]`, `axs[1, 0]`, `axs[1, 1]` — and plotted independently. In the capstone, four related delivery charts share one figure instead of appearing as four separate figures.
Pattern 2: plt.subplot(131/132/133) — a side-by-side row

`plt.subplot(131)`, `plt.subplot(132)`, and `plt.subplot(133)` each hold a different chart side by side in one figure, and `plt.suptitle()` adds one title over the whole figure. In the capstone, three delivery charts can sit side by side under one shared title instead of as three separate figures.

blocks.code:
# Pattern 1: 2×2 grid
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)
axs[0, 0].bar(zones, avg_times)
axs[0, 0].set_title('Avg delivery time by zone')
axs[0, 1].bar(shifts, shift_avg)
axs[0, 1].set_title('Avg delivery time by shift')
axs[1, 0].bar(zones, order_counts)
axs[1, 0].set_title('Order count by zone')
axs[1, 1].hist(delivery_times, bins=10)
axs[1, 1].set_title('Distribution of delivery times')
plt.tight_layout()

# Pattern 2: side-by-side row
plt.subplot(131)
plt.bar(zones, avg_times)
plt.subplot(132)
plt.bar(shifts, shift_avg)
plt.subplot(133)
plt.hist(delivery_times, bins=10)
plt.suptitle('Delivery Performance -- Last Quarter')
plt.tight_layout()

annotations.text: Pattern 1: subplots(2, 2) returns a 2-D array of axes; address each by [row, col].
Pattern 2: subplot(1, 3, n) places charts side by side; suptitle() adds one shared title.

remediation_steps.title: describe() output and choosing mean vs median
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about interpreting describe() output and selecting the right statistic. Here's the key contrast.

blocks.text: describe() computes count, mean, std, min, 25th percentile, 50th percentile (the median), 75th percentile, and max for a Series or DataFrame column. The 50% row in describe()'s output is the median. In the capstone, running describe() on Ikeja's `delivery_time` column returns a mean of 52 minutes and a median of 38 minutes. (In the full dataset, beyond this sample, a handful of deliveries took over three hours, pulling the mean to 52 minutes while the median stays at 38 minutes.)

The mean is pulled upward by extreme observations; the median is not. When a few deliveries took over three hours, the mean rises to 52 minutes even though most deliveries were around 38 minutes. (In the full dataset, beyond this sample, a handful of deliveries took over three hours, pulling the mean to 52 minutes while the median stays at 38 minutes.) For the business question — which zones miss the target and by how much — the median (38 minutes) better represents a typical delivery than the mean (52 minutes).

remediation_steps.title: Both multi-panel patterns: subplots(2,2) and subplot(131/132/133)
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about both plt.subplots(2, 2) and plt.subplot(131/132/133). Here are both patterns.

blocks.text: `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` returns one Figure and a 2-D NumPy array of four Axes objects. Each axes is addressed by its row and column index: `axs[0, 0]` is the top-left, `axs[0, 1]` is the top-right, `axs[1, 0]` is the bottom-left, and `axs[1, 1]` is the bottom-right. You call plotting methods on each axes independently — `axs[0, 0].bar(...)`, `axs[0, 1].hist(...)` — and `plt.tight_layout()` prevents the panels from overlapping.

A common mistake is calling `plt.subplots(2, 2)` but then plotting with `plt.bar(...)` instead of `axs[row, col].bar(...)`. Using the global `plt` functions after subplots() plots into the last active axes, not the one you intend. Always address the specific axes object by index.

`plt.subplot(131)` means: 1 row, 3 columns, activate panel 1. `plt.subplot(132)` activates panel 2, and `plt.subplot(133)` activates panel 3. Each call makes that panel current, so the next plotting call draws into it. `plt.suptitle("Delivery Performance -- Last Quarter")` adds one title above all three panels.

remediation_steps.title: Selecting the right multi-panel layout for the capstone findings
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked which layout best fits the capstone findings. Here is how to choose.

blocks.text: `plt.subplots(2, 2)` creates a 2×2 grid — use it when you have four related charts to show together. `plt.subplot(131/132/133)` creates a 1×3 side-by-side row — use it when three charts belong together in a single row. Both patterns produce one figure with multiple axes; the choice depends on how many charts you have and how they relate.

For the capstone, four delivery charts (by zone, by shift, order count, distribution) fit naturally into a 2×2 grid with `plt.subplots(2, 2)`. Three of those charts can instead sit side by side with `plt.subplot(131/132/133)` and a shared title from `plt.suptitle("Delivery Performance -- Last Quarter")`. Either layout turns separate charts into one coherent figure.
